deep.reconstruction:
The page is a set of lecture or seminar notes on foundations. It has three items.

(1) Identity of geometries; continuation of the previous page. Two geometries count as identical if there is a bijection between their elements under which every theorem of one holds in the other. Hilbert's example: the points of the Euclidean plane or space can be mapped bijectively onto a line segment. Modern form: |R^n| = |[0,1]| = 2^aleph_0, which is Cantor's result. Such a bijection is not continuous. The resulting segment-with-structure is still 'Euclidean geometry' provided one also transports every axiom, i.e. every relation (incidence, betweenness, congruence), along the bijection. Hilbert's moral: the concept of a geometry is independent of the names given to its elements. This is the structuralist or implicit-definition view: a theory is fixed only up to isomorphism of models (transport of structure).

(2) Methodological remark. There is no difference between analysis and geometry in so far as both aim to reach simple, fixed, traditional forms. Looking for what is common and softening oppositions is 'not only positive and Christian, but also the highest scientific principle'. A marginal addition gives the reason: experience shows that the essential ideas of the old theory always find their place in the new one. There is no mathematics to reconstruct here.

(3) Example of a bounded plane domain with boundary points that cannot be reached from the inside. This is the comb, or slit square. Take Q = (0,1)^2 and remove the vertical slits S_n = {1/2^n} x (0, h] for n = 1, 2, 3, ... (h < 1). The figure shows slits at x = 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and implies the rest ('usw.' is my addition). The domain is G = Q minus the union of the S_n. Hilbert: all points inside the square except those on the slits belong to the interior. G is open and connected: go around the tops of the slits.

My completion of the implicit argument: let P = (0, y0) with 0 <= y0 < h. P lies on the boundary of G, since it is the limit of interior points (1/2^n + 1/2^(n+1), y0). Now suppose a continuous path gamma: [0,1) -> G runs from an interior point with x-coordinate > 1/2^N to P. Its x-coordinate must pass every value 1/2^n for n > N. While it stays within distance < h - y0 of P, its height is < h at those moments, so it would lie on a slit. That is a contradiction. So such P cannot be reached by any arc in G: it is an inaccessible boundary point. By contrast, points (0, y) with y > h, and points on the slits themselves, are accessible. This domain is the standard illustration of the difference between boundary points and accessible boundary points. Such points matter for the Dirichlet problem and for boundary behaviour of conformal maps. The context pages discuss Kirchhoff's faulty uniqueness proof for potentials and non-Jordan curves separating the plane.
errors: 'An dessen Grenzpunkte man von Innen her überhaupt nicht herankommen kann' needs qualification. Every boundary point is a limit of interior points. What fails is approach along a continuous path (accessibility). Also, only the left-edge points (0,y) below the slit height h, including the corner (0,0), are inaccessible. Points on the left edge above the slit tips, and the slit points, are accessible. Hilbert does not state this restriction.
The figure shows only four slits, at 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. The example needs infinitely many slits accumulating at the left edge. This is implicit but unstated.

Item (1) is correct in substance, but the bijection plane -> segment (Cantor) is necessarily discontinuous. This is harmless, since only the transported axioms matter and not the topology of the segment.

results.what: A geometry is determined only up to bijective transport of structure; Euclidean points can be relabelled as points of a segment if all axioms are carried along (independence from the naming of elements).
results.modern_name: Implicit definition / structuralist view of axiom systems; isomorphism invariance of models; equicardinality |R^n| = |[0,1]|
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (the 'Tische, Stühle, Bierseidel' remark, c. 1891; Grundlagen der Geometrie 1899; Frege-Hilbert correspondence); the cardinality fact to Cantor (1877)

results.what: Methodological principle of unifying analysis and geometry, seeking what is common, and keeping old theories inside new ones.
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert's general philosophy (e.g. Paris 1900 address, 'Naturerkennen und Logik' 1930)

results.what: Comb (slit-square) domain whose left-edge boundary points below the slit tips cannot be reached by any path from the interior.
results.modern_name: Inaccessible boundary points; comb domain (prime-end example)
results.usually_credited_to: Schoenflies (accessible/erreichbare points, Bericht über die Mengenlehre 1900/1908) and Carathéodory (prime ends, 1913); the comb is folklore in that literature

deep.surprise_reason: Every item is either Hilbert's well-known foundational stance or a standard example. The comb domain with inaccessible boundary points belongs to the Schoenflies/Carathéodory circle of ideas around 1900-1913. Hilbert, whose interests included the Dirichlet problem and Jordan curves, plausibly used it in lectures. There is no evidence it precedes Schoenflies, and the page gives no proof.

checkable.asserts: The slit positions x = 1/2^n accumulate at the left edge x = 0, so infinitely many slits lie arbitrarily close to it.
The gaps between consecutive slits sum to the width 1/2 to the left of the first slit. A path reaching x = 0 must cross every x = 1/2^n.
The midpoints x = 3/2^(n+2) between slits are interior points tending to (0, y0), so left-edge points are boundary points even though they are inaccessible by paths.

transcription_corrections: Margin addition: 'in den neuen Theorie' is probably 'in den neuen Theorien' (or 'der neuen Theorie'); the handwriting is cramped.

Figure labels read 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 under the slits, with the slits rising from the bottom edge to roughly two-thirds of the height, not to the top. The transcription's 'senkrechte Striche vom unteren Rand nach innen' is correct.
'positiv und christlich': the image reads 'positiv' (the final letter resembles 'o'); the transcription is correct.
